[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood, i'm the account lead here, with me is liam who is our solutions eng and he will do the deep dive, hows everyone doing?
[00:10] Evan: good thanks, excited to see this, been looking at migration options from our current stack with openai and a couple experiments with anthro- with anthropic and together.ai as well, so hoping to see one-to-one parity and where the gaps are.
[00:27] Maya: perfect, that's exactly what we'll cover; we'll show the redwood api and console, and the optimize recommendations for cost/latency. quick ask, priya, did you share the sample prompt set?
[00:35] Priya: yes, i uploaded the prompts.csv to the shared drive this morning, and there's a little notes doc on edge cases.
[00:40] Liam: great, i'll reference that. just to set expectations, we'll show endpoints, model mappings, function-calling behavior, streaming notes, and then talk about dedicated/private options for PII workloads. sound good?
[00:49] Ava: yep sounds good.
[00:52] Liam: ok jumping in — on the left i have an openai example request, so folks familiar with the completions/chat completions flow —
[01:03] [screen share starts, faint typing noises]
[01:10] Liam: openai chat example uses messages + model gpt-4 style names; anthropic uses a different prompt format (claude style) and together has their own api -- mapping is mostly syntactic. in redwood we expose a unified api that accepts chat/messages, simple text generation, embeddings, and reranking. so first step is mapping model names — e.g., gpt-4 -> redwood-model/gpt4-compat (we call out "compat" variants)
[01:35] Evan: ok are those drop-in identical behavior wise? the sampling defaults and system messages?
[01:41] Liam: good question — compatibility variants aim to match logits and sampling defaults but there are differences. patches: you can override temperature, top_p, max_tokens exactly like openai. some behaviors like stop-sequence handling for anthropic style might need small prompt changes — we'll include examples in the parity sheet.
[01:58] [brief crosstalk, keyboard]
[02:10] Priya: how about function-calling? we use function-calling heavily in prod to structure extraction. openai's func call is very specific.
[02:18] Liam: right — redwood supports function/tool calling and structured outputs. we support both explicit function schemas similar to openai and also a lighter-weight tool call pattern. important differences: our tool calls include provenance metadata and optional streaming of intermediate tokens while invoking external functions. small transcription note, sometimes our docs say "function schema" as "func schema" so watch for that.
[02:40] Evan: and streaming behaviour? we've got a realtime UI that expects delta tokens.
[02:45] Liam: yes — redwood supports chunked streaming; you can stream tokens identical to openai's chunk model, and we also support event-stream metadata for partial tool calls. caveat: when using dedicated on-prem pools with strict networking, the initial handshake might add small latency, but token stream is continuous once established.
[03:05] Sam: how about latency and batching — we see p95 token latency spikes under load.
[03:12] Liam: that is a big one — redwood's runtime does continuous batching and automatic KV cache for prefixes. for mapping, if you set batch size similar to your current setup you'll often get improved throughput and similar or better p95. in the parity doc we'll show recommended batch and sequence length settings per model. (i said kv cash earlier — sometimes the transcript tool spells it "kv cash")
[03:35] Priya: quantization — we currently use 4-bit quant models through together.ai experiments; can redwood run quantized weights?
[03:44] Liam: yes, redwood supports quantization profiles on the serving nodes, and we recommend model-specific profiles. if you're on hosted redwood we manage quantized variants; on dedicated/private you can opt for customer-managed quant profiles. note: there can be small quality delta, but cost/perf improves a lot.
[04:05] [00:04:05 noise]
[04:20] Ava: security questions: we need SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration.
[04:25] Maya: absolutely — we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. we also have SOC2 type 2 and can provide the audit package. i'll attach the security pack after this call.
[04:40] Priya: for data residency and on-prem, is private deployment fully air-gapped?
[04:45] Liam: yes — private can be fully on-prem with the control plane in your VPC or completely air-gapped with customer-managed keying. the tradeoff is you manage updates; we provide tooling. we'll call out the network diagram in the security doc.
[04:58] Evan: can we run the same prompt set across openai and redwood to compare outputs programmatically?
[05:04] Liam: totally — that's our suggested POC approach. we'll help set up benchmark harness that runs your sample prompts against openai/anthropic/together and redwood-hosted and returns per-response metrics (latency, token counts, detokenized diffs) and quality flags.
[05:20] [pause, typing]
[05:35] Liam: quick demo of code: here's an example node/python snippet calling redwood.chat.create() — it's basically the same fields: messages, functions, temperature. we also show how to configure streaming in the sdk.
[05:52] [screen scrolls - some words misread in the transcript]
[06:05] Maya: i want to point out the console — on the redwood console you can see per-route token breakdown, cost estimation, and the optimize suggestions which will propose batching and quantization settings.
[06:20] Ava: is optimize automated? can it run on our traffic?
[06:24] Liam: optimize can run in two ways: offline suggestions from historical logs and an online adaptive mode that recommends changes and can auto-apply safe tuning on dedicated pools with guardrails. it's opt-in.
[06:38] Priya: any gotchas on system/prompt tokens accounting? sometimes openai's tokenization differs and that affected our billing.
[06:45] Liam: yes, tokenizers differ — redwood reports both raw tokenization and normalized token metrics, and in the parity sheet we'll note where counts diverge (esp for multilingual prompts).
[06:58] Evan: curious about model fallback — if primary model hits quota can redwood auto-route to a cheaper variant?
[07:05] Liam: yes, smart routing policies allow you to set fallbacks by latency or cost. for example you can route to a gpt4-compat -> gpt4-small-compat fallback, with automatic rewriters for prompt differences.
[07:20] Sam: licensing and pricing — are we comparing hosted per-token to openai? what about reserved dedicated nodes pricing?
[07:27] Maya: hosted is usage-based (similar token pricing tiers) we will send a pricing sheet with hosted per-token numbers and reserved capacity monthly commitments for dedicated. usually dedicated becomes attractive at predictable high volume; we'll include an example TCO calc in the follow-up.
[07:40] Priya: what about model updates and pinning? we can't have silent weight changes in prod.
[07:45] Liam: you can pin model versions and manage rollouts — canary deploys and A/B test with automatic fallback. we also expose checksums and model version tags in the console.
[07:58] Ava: any example of mapping a specific together.ai model to redwood?
[08:05] Liam: yes — together.huge-v1 maps to redwood-model/together-compat-huge-v1 which is tuned to match generation characteristics; we'll include exact param mapping and sampling defaults in the parity spreadsheet.
[08:22] [longer pause while screen share switches]
[08:50] Liam: demo: running a sample suite — starting first 50 prompts against redwood-hosted gpt4-compat — showing p50/p95 latency and token delta alongside openai run. you can see here p95 is similar, cost is about 10-20% lower because of batching and prefix caching. this will vary with prompt length.
[09:18] Priya: nice, do you have the raw csv so we can run stats?
[09:22] Liam: yes, the benchmark outputs a csv and a perf dashboard link; i'll share that.
[09:30] Evan: about function-calling accuracy — if the schema mismatches slightly do you do auto-mapping?
[09:36] Liam: we provide small shims in the sdk to translate schemas and we recommend a short script to normalize function names and arg structures. in most cases it's few-line changes.
[09:50] Maya: ok I'm going to summarize the risks and gaps we saw: 1) a few prompt-level tweaks for anthropic-style prompts 2) small tokenization differences in some multilingual cases 3) quantization may need quality evals for certain models. nothing blocker but needs POC validation.
[10:12] Evan: that's fair. what's the typical POC timeline?
[10:17] Maya: for a standard parity POC we do 2-3 weeks: week 1 setup & data ingest, week 2 benchmark runs & quality evals, week 3 tuning and dedicated sizing conversation. we can accelerate if you provide prompts and traffic profile today.
[10:32] Priya: we can start week of the 28th — that works.
[10:35] Maya: great, we'll schedule the POC kickoff.
[10:40] Sam: legal and procurement — we'll need the standard m-ssa and DPAs.
[10:44] Maya: noted, i'll loop in legal and send templates; also attaching SOC2 and network diagram.
[10:51] Ava: any red flags on migration efforts you've seen?
[10:55] Liam: biggest is lack of test harness — i.e., teams try to swap models in production without side-by-side testing. we recommend running a canary and the bench harness in parallel for a few days. also watch streaming timeouts and connection pooling for high QPS.
[11:10] Priya: on instrumentation, does redwood emit trace ids we can correlate with our app logs?
[11:15] Liam: yes, we emit request IDs and support trace hooks for distributed tracing. we'll share the tracing guide.
